warmup.q: A program wrote 500,000 payment notes into Redis, each set to vanish 3 seconds later. Three seconds later, someone asks Redis for one of them with GET idem:250000. What comes back, and is the memory of all 500,000 notes free yet?
options: The old note: Redis clears out expired keys only once a second, in one sweep
Nothing (Redis's nil, which means no value), and the memory of all 500,000 notes is already free
Nothing, but most of the 500,000 notes are still in memory for about another second
Nothing, but only once a walk through all the keys (the SCAN command) has reached that note
warmup.why: Before Redis runs a command, it checks the deadline of the key that the command touches. So the GET deletes that one note and answers nothing. The other notes are removed by a cleanup round that runs 10 times a second, in slices of at most 25 ms, and on the lab server it needed about 1.1 seconds to reclaim all 500,000. There's no once-a-second sweep that could hand back an old note, and SCAN plays no part. The second section takes this apart.

sections.h: Giving a key a deadline: TTLs, and the commands that drop them
sections.html:
Let's start with the café's note. A card reader that loses its connection sends the same payment again. So each payment carries a ticket number, and the payments app stores it in Redis under a key such as idem:7f3a when the payment arrives. (A key is the name Redis keeps a value under, like the label on a drawer.) If the same ticket number comes back within 24 hours, the app finds the key and sends back the first answer, instead of charging the card again. That ticket is called an idempotency key. Idempotent means that doing something twice has the same effect as doing it once.

After 24 hours, no retry can come, and the key is garbage. At 35 payments a second, that's 3 million new keys a day.

Without help from Redis, we'd clean up ourselves. We'd store the creation time in each value, and run a job that lists every key with SCAN, a page at a time, and deletes the old ones. That job reads 3 million keys a day, and it runs on Redis's one thread. (Inside an in-memory store: how Redis executes commands showed that a single path of work runs every command, one at a time.) Any key the job misses stays forever.

So Redis lets you give a key a deadline. SET idem:7f3a pending EX 86400 stores the value and says "delete this 86,400 seconds from now". Redis turns that into a fixed moment, a Unix timestamp in milliseconds (computers count time from the start of 1970), and keeps it with the key. It also keeps a second table that holds only the keys that have a deadline, called the expires index. INFO keyspace shows both counts: keys=2,expires=1. The time a key has left is its TTL, short for time to live. TTL reports it in seconds, PTTL in milliseconds, and EXPIRETIME returns the deadline itself.

Redis gets rid of keys in two ways. Expiry removes keys whose deadline has passed. Eviction removes keys that Redis picks itself when its memory is full. Both run on the same single thread, between and before your commands, and the rest of the lesson fills in how.

A few rules cause most TTL bugs:

  • A plain SET replaces the value and drops the TTL, so the key now lives forever. Add KEEPTTL (Redis 6.0 and later) to keep the old deadline. Commands that change a value in place, such as INCR, which adds one to a number, keep it.
  • EXPIRE on a key that already has a TTL replaces the deadline. Since Redis 7.0, it takes NX (only if there's no TTL yet), XX (only if there is one), GT (only if the new deadline is later) and LT (only if it's earlier).
  • PERSIST removes the TTL. TTL answers -1 for a key without one, and -2 for a key that doesn't exist.
  • A TTL belongs to a whole key. To expire single fields of a hash, Redis 7.4 added HEXPIRE. Valkey 9.0 added the same family of commands. (Valkey is a free copy of Redis that split off from it in 2024.)

A plain SET makes a key live forever. Say KEEPTTL when you mean to keep the deadline.

A deadline is only a number stored next to the key, though. Next, we'll see who acts on it, and when.

try.expect: The first TTL prints (integer) 86400 and PTTL about (integer) 86399999. After the plain SET idem:7f3a done, TTL prints (integer) -1: the key now lives forever. SET ... KEEPTTL keeps the deadline that the SET ... EX 86400 before it gave the key, so the next TTL is back near 86400. INCR keeps the 60-second TTL from EXPIRE, so TTL auths:card:7 still prints (integer) 60. EXPIRE ... 30 GT answers (integer) 0, because 30 seconds isn't later than 60, and EXPIRE ... 600 GT answers (integer) 1. EXPIRE ... NX answers 0, because the key already has a TTL. After PERSIST, TTL is -1, and for a missing key it's -2. INFO keyspace ends with db0:keys=2,expires=1,...: two keys, one of them in the expires index.

sections.h: When an expired key really leaves memory
sections.html:
The 3 million notes from the last section each have their own deadline, somewhere in the next 24 hours. Redis has to delete each one at about the right moment, on one thread.

The obvious design is a timer for every key. Three million timers cost memory, and they would all go off on that one thread. The next idea is a sweep: once a second, check every key that has a deadline. That's 3 million checks every second, and while the sweep runs, no client is served, because it shares the thread with every command. (A client is any program that sends Redis commands.)

Picture a small library with one librarian, where some books carry a return-by date. The books are the keys, the return-by date is the TTL, and the librarian is Redis's one thread. She sets no alarms, and neither does Redis. It does two cheap things instead.

The first is lazy expiry. Every command that touches a key checks the key's deadline first. If the deadline has passed, Redis deletes the key right there and behaves as if it had never existed. That's the librarian checking the date on a book before she hands it over, and taking it away if it's overdue. It costs one comparison per command, and it means no client ever reads an expired value. On its own, it would leak memory: most payment notes are written once and never read again, so nothing would ever look at them.

The second is active expiry, a cleanup round on the main thread. Ten times a second (the hz setting, 10 by default), it walks the expires index from where it stopped last time, checks 20 keys and deletes the expired ones. If more than 10% of that batch had expired, there's probably more to do, so it takes another batch at once. It stops when a batch comes back mostly clean, or when it has used 25 ms, a quarter of the 100 ms between rounds. That's the librarian walking a few shelves now and then, walking on while she keeps finding overdue books, but never for more than a quarter of her time. So a few expired keys cost almost nothing, and many get the thread's full attention, in slices short enough that clients are still served in between. The picture breaks on scale: a librarian checks books one at a time, while Redis checks thousands of keys in a few milliseconds.

So an expired key becomes invisible at once, and leaves memory a little later. The lab server showed both, with 500,000 notes that shared one deadline. A GET answered nothing in the first check after the deadline, and that GET deleted exactly one key. The count of expired keys went from 0 to 1, while DBSIZE, which counts the keys in Redis, still said 500,001. The cleanup rounds then removed about 400,000 keys a second, and memory fell from 40 MB to 2 MB in about 1.1 seconds.

Those deletions are work on the main thread, so a mass expiry slows every client down for a moment. The next lesson, Caching patterns and stampedes, shows how to spread deadlines out.

Expiry only removes keys whose time is up. Next, we'll see what happens when keys arrive faster than they expire, and memory runs out.

sections.h: A full Redis says no: maxmemory and noeviction
sections.html:
Some keys never get a deadline, and some arrive faster than their deadlines pass. Either way, Redis keeps growing, and a cache is the usual case. (A cache is a store of copies kept close by, so they're quick to fetch.) By default, nothing stops the growth. On 64-bit systems, the maxmemory setting is 0, which means no limit. Redis grows until it reaches the memory limit of the container or machine it runs in. Then the out-of-memory killer, the part of Linux that ends a program when memory runs out, stops it. In Docker, you see exit code 137. Every client loses its connection at once, and a Redis that doesn't save its data to disk comes back empty.

The fix is to give Redis a budget: maxmemory 4gb in its settings file, or CONFIG SET maxmemory 4gb while it runs. Before Redis runs a command that can add data (SET, HSET, LPUSH, INCR and many more), it compares its memory use with the limit. Under the limit, the command runs. Over it, the eviction policy, the setting that says what to do when memory is full, decides.

The default policy is noeviction: refuse the write with an error, and keep every key. The lab's small server has a 4 MB limit and already uses 1.41 MB when it's empty. About 2,300 values of 1 KB fit, and then the next write fails:

(error) OOM command not allowed when used memory > 'maxmemory'.

OOM stands for out of memory. Reads keep working, and so do DEL and UNLINK, which delete keys. Refusing writes is the right default for data you can't afford to lose. If payment notes vanished without a word, a retried payment would be charged twice, as in the opening. An error at least gets noticed.

Two details about the limit. The check runs before each command, so the command itself can push memory past it: in one run, the lab server stopped at 4,218,576 bytes against a limit of 4,194,304. A single command that builds a big value, such as SUNIONSTORE (combine two sets into a new key) over two large sets, can overshoot by far more.

And maxmemory is compared with what Redis's memory allocator has handed out, used_memory. Linux counts something bigger, used_memory_rss, which includes fragmentation: gaps between blocks of memory that can't be reused yet. Some buffers aren't counted at all, and a background save, when Redis writes its data to disk, can need extra memory (Persistence and replication explains both). So set maxmemory well below the container's limit, and graph both numbers.

Give every Redis a maxmemory, well below the memory of the machine it runs on.

Refusing writes is right for notes you can't lose. A cache can lose entries, so it should make room instead. But which key should go?

sections.h: Choosing what to throw away: LRU, LFU and newer bets
sections.html:
When memory is full, a cache has to guess which key it will need least soon, and throw that one out. Back in the library, the shelves are full and a new book arrives. Which book goes to the basement? Every eviction policy answers with a different kind of evidence about the past.

FIFO, first in, first out, removes the book that arrived first and ignores how often anyone reads it. Its bookkeeping is one queue, and it throws popular books out on schedule. LRU, least recently used, removes the book nobody has opened for longest. LFU, least frequently used, removes the book opened the fewest times.

LRU is the usual choice. Why caches work: latency, locality and hit ratios found two places where it guesses badly: a loop over keys a little longer than the cache, and traffic where a few keys get most of the requests. It has three more weak spots. A one-time scan, such as a nightly report that reads every key once, makes every key look recent and pushes the popular ones out. Every hit, a request that finds its key in the cache, moves the key to the front of a list. The list has a lock, so only one thread at a time can change it, and busy threads queue for it. And a key asked for once travels the whole list before it leaves.

LFU shrugs off the scan: one more read can't push out keys with hundreds. But its counts must fade over time, or yesterday's popular key stays forever. Newer policies mix the two kinds of evidence, and Go deeper describes two well-known ones, ARC and W-TinyLFU.

The newest results come from counting one-hit wonders, keys that are asked for once and never again. A 2023 study, the S3-FIFO paper, looked at 6,594 traces, recordings of the requests real caches received. In the median trace, 26% of keys were one-hit wonders, and in a short stretch of a trace, one that touched only 10% of its keys, 72% were. So drop new keys quickly unless they prove themselves.

S3-FIFO does exactly that. New keys go into a small FIFO queue that holds 10% of the cache, and only keys asked for again while there move on to the main queue. S3-FIFO had the lowest average miss ratio, the share of requests a cache can't answer, on 10 of its 14 groups of traces. On 16 threads, it served six times the requests of a well-tuned LRU, because a hit only bumps a 2-bit counter.

SIEVE (2024) keeps one FIFO list and one visited bit per key. A hit sets the bit and moves nothing. To evict, a hand walks from the oldest key toward the newest, clears the bits it finds set, and evicts the first key whose bit is clear. Keys the hand spares stay where they are, and a new key that isn't asked for again goes the first time the hand reaches it. On Zipf traffic, its authors measured 13 to 18% fewer misses than LRU, at twice LRU's speed on 16 threads. Zipf traffic is the skewed pattern from Why caches work, where the second most popular key gets half the requests of the first. It's a close cousin of the clock sweep in the Storage track's lesson The buffer pool.

Those policies keep careful records about every key. Next, we'll see which one Redis uses, and how it gets by with almost no records at all.

code.title: PolicyDemo.java
code.html: package sfz.cache.l05.demo; import java.util.ArrayDeque; import java.util.Arrays; import java.util.HashMap; import java.util.HashSet; import java.util.LinkedHashMap; import java.util.Map; import java.util.Random; import java.util.Set; /** FIFO, LRU and SIEVE on the same Zipf requests, without and with one-time scans mixed in. No Docker needed. */ public class PolicyDemo { interface Policy { boolean access(int key); } public static void main(String[] args) { int n = 100_000; int[] zipf = zipfTrace(n, 1.0, 1_000_000, 7); int[] scans = withScans(zipf, n); System.out.println("miss ratio on the Zipf requests (alpha 1.0, 100,000 keys)"); System.out.println("cache workload FIFO LRU SIEVE"); for (int size : new int[] {1_000, 10_000}) { for (int[] trace : new int[][] {zipf, scans}) { System.out.printf("%,6d %-12s %6.1f%% %5.1f%% %5.1f%%%n", size, trace == zipf ? "Zipf" : "Zipf + scans", 100 * missRatio(trace, new Fifo(size), n), 100 * missRatio(trace, new Lru(size), n), 100 * missRatio(trace, new Sieve(size), n)); } } } /** Misses among the Zipf requests after a warm-up; scan keys (above n) are replayed but not counted. */ static double missRatio(int[] trace, Policy policy, int n) { long counted = 0, misses = 0; for (int i = 0; i < trace.length; i++) { boolean hit = policy.access(trace[i]); if (i >= trace.length / 5 && trace[i] <= n) { counted++; if (!hit) misses++; } } return (double) misses / counted; } /** FIFO: evict the key that was inserted first; a hit changes nothing. */ static final class Fifo implements Policy { final int capacity; final ArrayDeque<Integer> queue = new ArrayDeque<>(); final Set<Integer> cached = new HashSet<>(); Fifo(int capacity) { this.capacity = capacity; } public boolean access(int key) { if (cached.contains(key)) return true; if (cached.size() >= capacity) cached.remove(queue.pollFirst()); queue.addLast(key); cached.add(key); return false; } } /** LRU: a hit moves the key to the newest end; evict from the oldest end. */ static final class Lru implements Policy { final Map<Integer, Boolean> map; Lru(int capacity) { map = new LinkedHashMap<>(16, 0.75f, true) { @Override protected boolean removeEldestEntry(Map.Entry<Integer, Boolean> eldest) { return size() > capacity; } }; } public boolean access(int key) { if (map.get(key) != null) return true; map.put(key, Boolean.TRUE); return false; } } /** SIEVE: one FIFO list and a visited bit. A hit only sets the bit; the hand evicts the first unvisited key. */ static final class Sieve implements Policy { static final class Node { final int key; boolean visited; Node newer, older; Node(int key) { this.key = key; } } final int capacity; final Map<Integer, Node> nodes = new HashMap<>(); Node head, tail, hand; // head: newest, tail: oldest Sieve(int capacity) { this.capacity = capacity; } public boolean access(int key) { Node node = nodes.get(key); if (node != null) { node.visited = true; // no move, no lock needed in a concurrent version return true; } if (nodes.size() >= capacity) evict(); node = new Node(key); // new keys always enter at the head node.older = head; if (head != null) head.newer = node; head = node; if (tail == null) tail = node; nodes.put(key, node); return false; } void evict() { Node o = hand != null ? hand : tail; while (o.visited) { // spare visited keys, clear their bit, keep walking o.visited = false; o = o.newer != null ? o.newer : tail; // past the head: start again from the tail } hand = o.newer; // the next eviction resumes here if (o.newer != null) o.newer.older = o.older; else head = o.older; if (o.older != null) o.older.newer = o.newer; else tail = o.newer; nodes.remove(o.key); } } /** After every 50,000 requests, a one-time scan of 5,000 keys nobody asks for again. */ static int[] withScans(int[] zipf, int n) { int[] out = new int[zipf.length + zipf.length / 50_000 * 5_000]; int next = n + 1, j = 0; for (int i = 0; i < zipf.length; i++) { out[j++] = zipf[i]; if ((i + 1) % 50_000 == 0) for (int s = 0; s < 5_000; s++) out[j++] = next++; } return out; } static int[] zipfTrace(int n, double alpha, int length, long seed) { double[] cdf = new double[n]; double total = 0; for (int k = 1; k <= n; k++) total += Math.pow(k, -alpha); double running = 0; for (int k = 1; k <= n; k++) { running += Math.pow(k, -alpha) / total; cdf[k - 1] = running; } cdf[n - 1] = 1.0; Random random = new Random(seed); int[] trace = new int[length]; for (int i = 0; i < length; i++) { int k = Arrays.binarySearch(cdf, random.nextDouble()); trace[i] = (k >= 0 ? k : -k - 1) + 1; } return trace; } }

No Docker needed. */ fun main() { val n = 100_000 val zipf = zipfTrace(n, 1.0, 1_000_000, 7) val scans = withScans(zipf, n) println("miss ratio on the Zipf requests (alpha 1.0, 100,000 keys)") println("cache workload FIFO LRU SIEVE") for (size in listOf(1_000, 10_000)) { for ((name, trace) in listOf("Zipf" to zipf, "Zipf + scans" to scans)) { println("%,6d %-12s %6.1f%% %5.1f%% %5.1f%%".format(size, name, 100 * missRatio(trace, Fifo(size), n), 100 * missRatio(trace, Lru(size), n), 100 * missRatio(trace, Sieve(size), n))) } } } private interface Policy { fun access(key: Int): Boolean } /** Misses among the Zipf requests after a warm-up; scan keys (above n) are replayed but not counted. */ private fun missRatio(trace: IntArray, policy: Policy, n: Int): Double { var counted = 0L var misses = 0L trace.forEachIndexed { i, key -> val hit = policy.access(key) if (i >= trace.size / 5 && key <= n) { counted++ if (!hit) misses++ } } return misses.toDouble() / counted } /** FIFO: evict the key that was inserted first; a hit changes nothing. */ private class Fifo(val capacity: Int) : Policy { private val queue = ArrayDeque<Int>() private val cached = HashSet<Int>() override fun access(key: Int): Boolean { if (key in cached) return true if (cached.size >= capacity) cached.remove(queue.removeFirst()) queue.addLast(key) cached.add(key) return false } } /** LRU: a hit moves the key to the newest end; evict from the oldest end. */ private class Lru(val capacity: Int) : Policy { private val map = object : LinkedHashMap<Int, Boolean>(16, 0.75f, true) { override fun removeEldestEntry(eldest: MutableMap.MutableEntry<Int, Boolean>) = size > capacity } override fun access(key: Int): Boolean { if (map[key] != null) return true map[key] = true return false } } /** SIEVE: one FIFO list and a visited bit. A hit only sets the bit; the hand evicts the first unvisited key. */ private class Sieve(val capacity: Int) : Policy { private class Node(val key: Int) { var visited = false var newer: Node? = null var older: Node? = null } private val nodes = HashMap<Int, Node>() private var head: Node? = null // newest private var tail: Node? = null // oldest private var hand: Node? = null override fun access(key: Int): Boolean { nodes[key]?.let { it.visited = true // no move, no lock needed in a concurrent version return true } if (nodes.size >= capacity) evict() val node = Node(key) // new keys always enter at the head node.older = head head?.newer = node head = node if (tail == null) tail = node nodes[key] = node return false } private fun evict() { var o = hand ?: tail!! while (o.visited) { // spare visited keys, clear their bit, keep walking o.visited = false o = o.newer ?: tail!! // past the head: start again from the tail } hand = o.newer // the next eviction resumes here if (o.newer != null) o.newer!!.older = o.older else head = o.older if (o.older != null) o.older!!.newer = o.newer else tail = o.newer nodes.remove(o.key) } } /** After every 50,000 requests, a one-time scan of 5,000 keys nobody asks for again. */ private fun withScans(zipf: IntArray, n: Int): IntArray { val out = ArrayList<Int>(zipf.size + zipf.size / 10) var next = n + 1 zipf.forEachIndexed { i, key -> out += key if ((i + 1) % 50_000 == 0) repeat(5_000) { out += next++ } } return out.toIntArray() } private fun zipfTrace(n: Int, alpha: Double, length: Int, seed: Long): IntArray { val total = (1..n).sumOf { it.toDouble().pow(-alpha) } var running = 0.0 val cdf = DoubleArray(n) { running += (it + 1.0).pow(-alpha) / total; running } cdf[n - 1] = 1.0 val random = Random(seed) return IntArray(length) { val k = cdf.binarySearch(random.nextDouble()) (if (k >= 0) k else -k - 1) + 1 } }

try.expect: FIFO, LRU and SIEVE missed 53.5%, 49.3% and 40.0% of requests with 1,000 slots, and 29.8%, 26.1% and 21.6% with 10,000. SIEVE missed 17 to 19% less than LRU, in line with its paper, and the LRU column matches the curve in Why caches work. With the scans at 10,000 slots, FIFO rose to 32.2% and LRU to 29.0%, while SIEVE stayed at 21.6%: scan keys arrive with their bit clear, so the hand evicts them before any key that was hit. At 1,000 slots, the scans changed little for any policy. A key the hand spares keeps its place in the list with its bit cleared, while LRU moves a key on every hit. Both versions print the same numbers.

sections.h: How Redis picks a victim: a small random sample
sections.html:
So which of these does Redis use? None of them exactly. A cache is allowed to lose entries, because a missing one only costs one slow trip to the database to fetch it again. So a cache should make room instead of refusing, and choose well. But Redis can't afford the bookkeeping most policies need. Exact LRU keeps every key in a linked list, a chain in which each entry points to its neighbors, and moves a key to the front on every read. That's two pointers, 16 bytes, per key. With 50 million keys, that's 800 MB of pointers, rewritten by the one thread that runs every command.

So Redis samples. Every key carries 24 bits that record when it was last used, in seconds. When Redis must free memory, it picks 5 keys at random (the maxmemory-samples setting). It adds them to the eviction pool, the 16 best candidates it has seen so far. Then it evicts the one that has been idle longest, and repeats until memory is under the limit. Old keys collect in the pool from round to round, so the result is close to true LRU, and 10 samples get closer still. In the library, that's a librarian who grabs five books at random and sends the one nobody has opened for longest to the basement.

The EvictionDemo program from the 4 MB Try it shows what that's worth. It keeps 200 hot keys, which it reads before each of four batches of 800 cold keys, written once and never read. Under allkeys-random, which evicts any key at random, 79 of the 200 hot keys were evicted in one run. Under allkeys-lru, all 200 survived, and most of the oldest batch was gone.

Redis's LFU (since 4.0) reuses the same 24 bits. They hold a counter that grows more slowly the bigger it gets (8 bits), and the time, in minutes, when it last faded (16 bits). About a million hits take the counter to its maximum, 255, and it drops by one for every minute nobody touches the key. A new key starts at 5, so it gets a chance before it's judged, and a scan adds at most one point to each key it reads. LRM, least recently modified (Redis 8.6), updates a key's time stamp only on writes, so a key that is read all day but never changed can still go. None of the newer policies from the last section is in Redis 8.10.

Every policy comes as allkeys-*, which considers every key, or volatile-*, which considers only keys with a TTL. A volatile-* policy on a server where no key has a TTL behaves exactly like noeviction. volatile-ttl evicts the key nearest its deadline.

Now we can explain the opening's double charge. The quick fix set allkeys-lru on the Redis that held the payment notes. Under memory pressure, Redis evicts whatever has been idle longest, and a 23-hour-old note is exactly that. The next retry of that payment found no note, and the card was charged again. For a cache, start with allkeys-lru, or allkeys-lfu when a few keys are very hot and scans happen.

Data gets noeviction and an alert. A cache gets allkeys-lru. Keep them in separate Redis servers.

That's as far as this lesson's tools go. Expiry and eviction decide when a key leaves, and sampling means Redis evicts an old key, not always the oldest. Neither one says where the next copy of a key comes from.

A hot key can only go when a whole sample, and the pool, hold nothing older, which is rare. In the demo, allkeys-lru kept all 200 hot keys, while allkeys-random lost 79 of them. One catch: the stamp counts whole seconds, so keys touched in the same second tie.

"" : ", then: " + error); if (error != null) break; } long hotLeft = hot.stream().filter(redis::exists).count(); StringBuilder cold = new StringBuilder(); for (int round = 0; round < 4; round++) { int left = 0; for (int i = 0; i < 800; i++) if (redis.exists("cold:" + round + ":" + i)) left++; cold.append(round == 0 ? "" : ", ").append(left); } System.out.println("hot keys left: " + hotLeft + " of 200"); System.out.println("cold keys left per batch: " + cold); System.out.println("evicted_keys: " + (stat(redis, "stats", "evicted_keys") - evictedBefore) + ", used_memory: " + stat(redis, "memory", "used_memory")); } } static long stat(RedisClient redis, String section, String field) { for (String line : redis.info(section).split("\r\n")) { if (line.startsWith(field + ":")) return Long.parseLong(line.substring(field.length() + 1).trim()); } throw new IllegalArgumentException(field); } }

opening:
Picture a busy café. You tap your card, and the card reader's connection drops before the answer comes back, so it sends the payment again. To make sure nobody pays twice, the payments app notes every payment it has seen in Redis, a program that holds data in a computer's memory. Each note is set to vanish after 24 hours.

One Saturday, Redis runs out of room, refuses new notes, and payments fail. The quick fix is one setting that tells Redis to throw old notes away when it's full. It works until a retried payment finds no note, and the customer pays twice.

It's easy to think a note vanishes the moment its time is up, and that a full store should make room. Both sound like common sense.

In Bitmaps, HyperLogLog, geo and the Redis 8 built-ins, we asked what a key costs. In this lesson, we'll watch keys pass their deadlines, fill a small Redis until it says no, and see how it picks what to drop. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a Redis full of payment notes that refused new ones, and a quick fix that charged a card twice. An expired key is invisible at once and leaves memory a little later. A full Redis refuses writes unless a policy tells it which keys to give up. Giving keys up is right for a cache and wrong for data like these notes.

If you can reach a Redis, run CONFIG GET maxmemory* and INFO stats. Check whether maxmemory is 0, and compare evicted_keys with expired_keys.

Next, we'll put Redis in front of a database as a cache, and find out why one key's deadline can send a hundred identical requests to the database at once.

compare.title: A TTL that survives the update, in Java and Kotlin

java.title: IdempotencyKeys.java
java.html: // a new payment request: claim its idempotency key for 24 hours, only if nobody has String claimed = redis.set(key, "pending", SetParams.setParams().nx().ex(86_400)); if (claimed == null) { return Outcome.DUPLICATE; // SET NX returns null when the key exists } // ... authorize with the issuer ... // record the result, but keep the deadline set above redis.set(key, "done:" + paymentId, SetParams.setParams().xx().keepTtl()); long secondsLeft = redis.ttl(key); // still about 86,400, not -1

compare.note: Both versions use Jedis, the Java library this track uses to talk to Redis, and send the same commands: SET ... NX EX 86400 to claim the note only if nobody has (NX), then SET ... XX KEEPTTL to record the result without losing the deadline (XX means only if the key exists). Leave out keepTtl(), and the second SET silently makes the key permanent, the leak that TTL answering -1 gives away. Kotlin must declare claimed as String?, a string that may be null: Jedis returns null when NX finds the key already there, and without the ? that null could slip into code that expects a value. Rate limiting and idempotency keys builds the full flow on this.

drill.title: Write chooseVictim from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. You have a List<String> keys, a Map<String, Long> lastUsed, an int samples and a Random random. Write String chooseVictim() the way Redis approximates LRU. Then compare with the answer. Why does Redis sample at all, instead of keeping its keys in order of use?

answer.html: String chooseVictim() { String victim = null; for (int i = 0; i < samples; i++) { String candidate = keys.get(random.nextInt(keys.size())); // a random key, O(1) if (victim == null || lastUsed.get(candidate) < lastUsed.get(victim)) { victim = candidate; // the oldest of the sample so far } } return victim; }

alt.html: fun chooseVictim(): String = (1..samples) .map { keys[random.nextInt(keys.size)] } // a random key, O(1) .minBy { lastUsed.getValue(it) } // the oldest of the sample

recap: A TTL is a fixed deadline stored with the key. A plain SET drops it, KEEPTTL keeps it, and commands that change a value in place, such as INCR and HSET, leave it alone.

An expired key is deleted lazily when a command touches it, and by a cleanup round that checks 20 keys at a time, 10 times a second, for at most 25 ms. It's invisible at once but can sit in memory for a while: 500,000 keys took about 1.1 seconds to reclaim.
maxmemory has no limit by default. The default policy, noeviction, refuses writes when memory is full and keeps every key.
Eviction policies bet on recency (LRU), frequency (LFU) or both. S3-FIFO and SIEVE drop one-hit wonders quickly and move nothing on a hit; SIEVE missed about 19% less than LRU in this lesson's demo.

Redis samples 5 keys into a pool of 16 and evicts the one idle longest (LRU), used least (LFU) or changed least recently (LRM, 8.6). Use noeviction for data and allkeys-lru for a cache, in separate servers.
The limit: expiry and eviction only decide when a key leaves. Sampling evicts an old key, not always the oldest, and nothing here brings a lost copy back.

explain.prompt: A teammate set EX 86400 on the payment notes and is surprised that DBSIZE sometimes counts notes whose 24 hours are up, and that writes started failing once Redis filled up. Explain both, and say what you'd change.
explain.answer: Redis doesn't delete a key at its deadline. Every command that touches a key checks the deadline first and deletes the key then, so no client ever reads an expired note. Notes nobody touches are removed by a cleanup round that runs 10 times a second and checks 20 keys with a TTL at a time. It goes on while it keeps finding expired ones, for at most 25 ms per round. Until that round reaches a note, the note still takes memory and still counts in DBSIZE. The failing writes come from the eviction policy. When memory reaches maxmemory, the default, noeviction, refuses writes instead of deleting anything. For these notes that's right, because losing one could charge a card twice. So I'd keep noeviction, size maxmemory for the write rate times the TTL with room to spare, alert when used_memory passes 80% of it, and move any cached copies to a separate Redis with allkeys-lru.

deeper.html:
The cleanup round has a second, faster mode. Before Redis goes back to waiting for commands, it may run a "fast" round that lasts at most 1 ms. It runs only when Redis estimates that at least 10% of the keys with a TTL have already expired, or when the last slow round hit its time limit. The slow round, 10 times a second, does most of the work. active-expire-effort (1 to 10, default 1) raises the batch size, the time budget and the share of expired keys the round accepts, all together. At 10, each batch checks 65 keys, a round may use 43% of the tick, and it keeps going until only 1% of a batch has expired.

INFO stats keeps the score: expired_keys counts every expiry, expired_keys_active the cleanup rounds' share, and expired_time_cap_reached_count the rounds that hit the 25 ms limit. Replicas, the copies of a Redis server that Persistence and replication sets up, never expire keys on their own. They wait for the main server to send a DEL, and until it arrives, they answer reads for an expired key with nil, like the main server.

The freeing itself happens on the main thread unless you say otherwise. lazyfree-lazy-expire yes hands expired values to bio_lazy_free, the background thread from Inside an in-memory store: how Redis executes commands, and lazyfree-lazy-eviction yes does the same for evicted keys. That matters when keys are big: expiring one hash with a million fields frees a lot of memory in one go.

The 24-bit LRU stamp counts seconds and wraps around after 2^24 seconds, about 194 days. Redis handles the wrap when it works out idle time, so a key idle for longer than that only looks less idle than it is. OBJECT IDLETIME shows the idle time in seconds, which is why it rarely shows anything but small numbers on a busy key.

One surprise while testing the eviction lab: a Lua script is checked against maxmemory only when it starts. If the server was over the limit then, the script's first write fails. Once a script has written anything, Redis lets it run to the end, because stopping it halfway would break its promise to run as one step (the Transactions track's lesson Serial execution: Redis MULTI, WATCH and Lua). A script that began under the limit wrote 100,000 keys of 1 KB into a server with maxmemory 4mb, and used_memory ended at 108 MB. A client that sends SET after SET sees the OOM error on time; one script can blow straight through the limit.

maxmemory-eviction-tenacity (default 10) limits how long one command may spend evicting before Redis moves the rest of the work to a background timer, so a burst of big writes can't stall one client for long. Set maxmemory-clients if a few clients with huge buffers could crowd out the data.

Two well-known policies mix recency and frequency. ARC (IBM, 2003) keeps one list for keys seen once and one for keys seen again, remembers the names of keys it recently evicted, and shifts space between the two lists whenever a remembered key comes back. On a scan-heavy database benchmark with a 4 GB cache, it hit 20% of requests where LRU hit 9.19%. Its adapting is a single number, the target size of the recency list, nudged up when a key evicted from the recency side comes back and down when one from the frequency side does. W-TinyLFU, the policy in Caffeine, a popular cache library for Java, puts a small LRU window in front of the main cache. A key leaving the window gets in only if a Count-min sketch (Bitmaps, HyperLogLog, geo and the Redis 8 built-ins named it), costing about 8 bytes per entry, says it's used more often than the key it would push out. The sketch ages by halving every counter after a fixed number of additions, which is how it forgets yesterday's hot keys, and Caffeine tunes the size of its window by trial and error while it runs.

S3-FIFO's ghost queue holds only the names of as many keys as the main queue, so a key that was demoted too early gets a second chance without costing a slot. The SIEVE authors list Dragonfly, another in-memory store that understands Redis's commands, among the systems that adopted SIEVE. And Twitter's study of its own caches found that plain FIFO did about as well as LRU for many workloads at the sizes it actually ran, with LRU pulling ahead mainly when a cache was too small.
